items.title: Treasure Trove
items.text: I aspire for this to become the most comprehensive educational resource list focused on free or low-cost resources. As I am someone who lives in the US, a handful of these resources will be aimed towards US citizens specifically. That being said, if anyone ever has resources I should add to the list regardless of country of origin, please email me at: tranquil.tyrant@gmail.com. Here are the resources:

items.title: 1. Crisis Support
items.text:
If you or someone near you is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number (911 in the US).

  • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US) — Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org, any time. Free and confidential, in English and Spanish.
  • Crisis Text Line — Text HOME to 741741 (US) to reach a trained crisis counselor by text.
  • The Trevor Project — Crisis support for LGBTQ+ young people by phone, text, and chat.
  • Trans Lifeline — Peer support run by and for trans people.
  • Veterans Crisis Line — Support for veterans, service members, and their families. Dial 988, then press 1.
  • National Domestic Violence Hotline — Support and safety planning for people experiencing abuse, by phone, text, and chat.
  • RAINN — The largest US anti-sexual-violence organization, with a confidential support hotline and online chat.
  • National Alliance for Eating Disorders Helpline — Support and referrals for eating disorders. (This replaces the former NEDA helpline, which has been disconnected.)
  • SAMHSA National Helpline — Free referral service for mental health and substance use treatment.
  • 211 — Connects you to local help with housing, food, utilities, and counseling.

items.title: International
items.text:
• International Suicide Hotlines (Open Counseling) — Country-by-country list of crisis lines.
  • Find a Helpline — Searchable directory of free, trusted helplines in many countries.
  • Befrienders Worldwide — Network of emotional support centers around the world.

items.title: 2. Therapy & Counseling
items.text:
• Mental Health Coalition Resources — Curated mental health education and support links.
  • Psychology Today Therapy Finder — Search therapists by location, specialty, insurance, and cost.
  • Open Path Collective — Lower-cost therapy sessions for people without insurance or with limited income.
  • FindTreatment.gov — SAMHSA's locator for mental health and substance use treatment facilities.
  • NAMI (National Alliance on Mental Illness) — Education, local support groups, and a helpline for people and families affected by mental illness.
  • Mental Health America — Free screening tools, articles, and a guide to finding help.
  • Inclusive Therapists — Directory centering therapists who serve marginalized and neurodivergent communities.
  • 7 Cups — Free peer listening and paid online therapy. Peer listeners are trained volunteers, not clinicians.

items.title: 3. Self-Care & Wellness Tools
items.text:
• Headspace — Guided meditation, sleep, and stress tools (subscription).
  • Insight Timer — Large library of free guided meditations and talks.
  • Smiling Mind — Free mindfulness programs for different ages.
  • MindShift CBT — Free app from Anxiety Canada teaching cognitive behavioral skills for anxiety.
  • Greater Good in Action — Science-based well-being practices from UC Berkeley.
  • Active Minds — Mental health awareness and peer support aimed at students.
  • The Jed Foundation — Mental health resources for teens and young adults.
  • Understood — Support for learning and thinking differences such as dyslexia and ADHD.
  • CHADD — Support and education for people with ADHD.
  • Mind (UK) — UK mental health charity with clear guides on conditions and treatments. International.
  • Beyond Blue (Australia) — Mental health information and support. International.

items.text:

  • LearnFree Courses — Free beginner-friendly lessons.

  • ReadWorks — Free reading passages and comprehension tools.
  • USA Learns — Free English and reading courses for adults.
  • EnGen — Career-aligned English language pathways. Access is usually through an organization or program.
  • Purdue OWL — Free writing, grammar, and citation help.
  • Paul's Online Math Notes — Free algebra, calculus, and differential equations notes.
  • CK-12 — Free K-12 STEM textbooks and practice.
  • GED.com — Official GED information, registration, and practice tests.
  • HiSET — Official information on the high school equivalency exam.
  • The Learning Scientists — Research-backed study strategies.
  • Northstar Digital Literacy — Free self-assessments and lessons in basic computer skills.
  • Duolingo — Free game-style language practice.
  • Anki — Free flashcard software using spaced repetition.
  • Bookshare — Accessible ebooks for people with print disabilities.
  • Learning Ally — Human-narrated audiobooks for dyslexia and other reading barriers.
  • Libby — Borrow ebooks and audiobooks from your public library. Library card

items.text:

  • Stanford Online — Free and paid courses from Stanford faculty.
  • Harvard Online — Harvard courses, including some free options. CS50 is a popular free start: cs50.harvard.edu.
  • Carnegie Mellon Open Learning Initiative (OLI) — Interactive courses with built-in practice. Independent learner courses are free for self-study.
  • OpenLearn (Open University, UK) — Free short courses across arts, science, and society. International.
  • Gresham College — Free public lectures by leading academics. International.
  • Oxford Podcasts and Lectures — Free lectures and talks from the University of Oxford. International.
  • Oxford Department for Continuing Education ⚠ — Public lectures and adult-learning content from Oxford. Check what is free.
  • ASU Universal Learner Courses — Low-cost college courses from Arizona State University that can lead to credit.
  • Study Hall — YouTube partnership with CrashCourse on college-foundation courses.
  • Modern States — Free courses that prepare you to earn college credit through CLEP exams.
  • Saylor Academy — Free, self-paced college-level courses.
  • NPTEL (India) — Engineering, science, and humanities lectures from the IITs. International.
  • SWAYAM (India) — India's government platform for free courses. International.
  • Academic Earth — Curated lists of free online courses from top universities. The site now also carries online-degree advertising.
  • Open Education Global — International network supporting open educational resources.
  • Smarthistory — Free art history articles and videos from prehistory to the present.

  • FutureLearn — UK-based platform with short courses in health, history, tech, and more. International.
  • Alison — Free certificate and diploma courses in business, IT, health, and languages.
  • LinkedIn Learning — Professional skills courses. Often free with a public library card. Library card

  • Grow with Google — Free career training and certificates in digital skills.
  • Microsoft Learn — Free self-paced training for Microsoft tools, cloud, and data.
  • freeCodeCamp — Free coding curriculum with projects and certifications.
  • The Odin Project — Free, project-based web development path.
  • Codecademy — Interactive coding lessons with free and paid tiers.
  • CreativeLive — Classes in photography, art, craft, and creative business (paid, with some free content).
  • Domestika — Project-based creative courses taught by working professionals (paid).
  • Skillshare — Creative and productivity classes by subscription.
  • Udemy — Marketplace of affordable courses on nearly any topic.
  • Wondrium (The Great Courses) — Professor-led video courses by subscription. The original Great Courses site is still online. Also on Kanopy through some libraries.
  • Open Culture: Free Online Courses — Directory of well over a thousand free courses and lectures.

items.title: STU-101 · Student Success 101
items.text: A 4-week, self-paced curriculum

items.title: Course at a glance
items.text:
Course code STU-101 Duration 4 weeks · about 5 hours per week (≈20 hours total) · 16 core sessions, with the capstone built across the course Format Self-guided. Every live or partner activity has a solo version, and every module has low-tech and no-tech options. Prerequisites None Support There is no instructor feedback loop, so each week has built-in self-checks (a confidence check at the start, a retrieval check at the end). You may also contact Killian with any questions or concerns. Free spine text OpenStax College Success (free web view and PDF): https://openstax.org/details/books/college-success

Pacing. Each week is a 10-minute start-of-week confidence check, four sessions of about 65 minutes, and a 15-minute end-of-week self-check, which comes to roughly 5 hours. Every session lists its read, watch, and listen items with a time estimate and a link to a free, official or publisher-hosted source.

items.title: Course learning objectives (CLOs)
items.text:
By the end of STU-101, students will be able to:

  1. Model self: Describe their own learning profile, strengths, and challenges, and articulate a personal motivation statement.
  2. Adopt a growth mindset: Apply growth-mindset thinking to setbacks and reframe fixed "I can't" statements.
  3. Set and govern goals: Set SMART goals and run a self-regulation cycle (forethought → performance → self-reflection).
  4. Learn how to learn: Apply evidence-based study strategies (retrieval practice, spaced practice, interleaving, effective note-taking).
  5. Plan time and work: Build a realistic weekly plan, break down large tasks (including when procrastination gets in the way), and manage a multi-course workload.
  6. Read and process academic text: Use structured reading (survey–question–read–recite–review) and annotate actively.
  7. Prepare for assessment: Use exam and assignment preparation routines that target understanding, not last-minute cramming.
  8. Sustain performance: Connect well-being, campus and community resources, and persistence to long-term success, and draft a personal success plan.

items.title: The four modules at a glance
items.text: Module Theme Core CLOs Capstone contribution 1 Foundations & Mindset 1–3 "About Me as a Learner" + SMART goals + Zimmerman cycle sheet 2 Learning How to Learn 4, 6 Strategy Toolkit card + spaced-practice schedule 3 Time, Procrastination & Systems 5, 7 Working weekly plan + chunked big task + exam/assignment prep plan 4 Well-being, Resources & Sustainability 8 (integrates all) Personal Student Success Plan (capstone)

items.title: Module 1 — Foundations & Mindset: "Who Am I as a Learner?"
items.text:
Theme: Before technique, identity. You can't regulate learning you haven't examined.

CLOs in play: 1, 2, 3

items.title: Learning objectives
items.text:
1. Identify their own learning profile: strengths, challenges, context, and past workarounds. (This is not a "learning styles" quiz. The research doesn't support matching study methods to styles, so the profile is about what actually helps you and what gets in your way.)
  2. Describe at least two ways their beliefs about ability (fixed vs. growth) shape their choices and persistence.
  3. Apply growth-mindset reframing to a real academic setback.
  4. Create at least three SMART goals for the coming weeks.
  5. Explain the three phases of Zimmerman's self-regulation cycle and place themselves within it.

items.title: Desired outcomes
items.text:
• A written "About Me as a Learner" profile naming at least 2 strengths, 2 challenges, and 1 current workaround.
  • One reframing exercise where a fixed "I can't" statement becomes "I can't yet, and here's the path."
  • A SMART goals sheet with at least 3 goals, each with a metric, deadline, and first action step.
  • A one-paragraph motivation statement ("why I'm here").
  • A one-page Zimmerman cycle sheet for one real goal: forethought (goal and plan), performance (strategy and how you'll monitor), self-reflection (what worked, what to change).

items.title: Sessions
items.text:
• Session 1 — The Learner Inventory (≈55 min)
  • Session 2 — Mindset: Fixed vs. Growth (≈55 min)
  • Session 3 — Motivation That Lasts (≈50 min)
  • Session 4 — Goals & Self-Regulation (≈60 min)

items.title: Module 2 — Learning How to Learn: "Study in a Way That Sticks"
items.text:
Theme: The craft. Replace low-yield habits (re-reading, highlighting) with high-yield, evidence-based ones.

CLOs in play: 4, 6

items.title: Learning objectives
items.text:
1. Analyze the difference between passive and active study, and rank common techniques by evidence.
  2. Apply retrieval practice (self-testing) and spaced practice to a real study session.
  3. Differentiate effective note-taking (Cornell, active annotation) from transcription.
  4. Apply a structured reading routine (Survey–Question–Read–Recite–Review) to academic text.
  5. Create a personal study-strategy toolkit matched to their Module 1 profile.

items.title: Desired outcomes
items.text:
• A completed self-test using retrieval, with a short reflection on what the test revealed.
  • A spaced-practice schedule for one subject (for example, study on Day 1, 3, and 7, not one 4-hour block).
  • One page of annotated notes using an active method (not transcription).
  • A one-paragraph reading log showing you ran Survey–Question–Read–Recite–Review on a real passage.
  • A Strategy Toolkit card listing your top 3 strategies with a specific use-case for each.

items.title: Sessions
items.text:
• Session 1 — The Evidence (≈70 min)
  • Session 2 — Retrieval & Spacing in Practice (≈65 min)
  • Session 3 — Notes That Work (≈65 min)
  • Session 4 — Reading Academic Text (≈65 min)

items.title: Module 3 — Time, Procrastination & Systems: "Make the Workload Manageable"
items.text:
Theme: The machinery. Turn intent into a repeatable weekly operating system, and handle the moments when you don't follow it.

CLOs in play: 5, 7

items.title: Learning objectives
items.text:
1. Analyze where their time actually goes (a one-week time audit).
  2. Apply a weekly planning routine that front-loads commitments and protects focus time.
  3. Explain procrastination as largely an emotion-regulation problem and apply at least two strategies for getting started.
  4. Break large tasks into sequenced, manageable steps with checkpoints, and prepare for an exam or assignment by working backward from the date.
  5. Evaluate common productivity tools and choose one stack that fits their system (not the hype).

items.title: Desired outcomes
items.text:
• A completed one-week time audit showing real vs. perceived time use.
  • A working weekly plan (one real week, not a fantasy week) with fixed commitments, blocked focus time, and a buffer.
  • A short priority-triage note for a busy week (urgent vs. important vs. delegable or droppable).
  • One large task broken down into at least 5 sequenced steps with interim checkpoints, plus one "if–then" start plan for the step you're most likely to avoid.
  • An exam or assignment prep plan for one real upcoming deadline: worked backward from the date, with three spaced sessions, one practice test, and a post-exam or post-assignment review prompt.
  • A one-line tool decision (one planner/calendar + one note system) with the reason it fits you.

items.title: Sessions
items.text:
• Session 1 — The Time Audit (≈60 min, plus tracking all week)
  • Session 2 — The Weekly Operating System, Triage & Tools (≈70 min)
  • Session 3 — Procrastination, Big Tasks & Small Steps (≈70 min)
  • Session 4 — Exams & Assignments Without Cramming (≈65 min)

items.title: Module 4 — Well-being, Resources & Sustainability: "Make It Last"
items.text:
Theme: The fuel. Success that burns you out isn't success. Integrate well-being, resources, and persistence into a plan you'll actually keep.

CLOs in play: 8 (integrating all)

items.title: Learning objectives
items.text:
1. Explain the evidence link between sleep, stress, and academic performance.
  2. Apply at least two evidence-based stress-regulation or recovery strategies.
  3. Identify the resources most relevant to their situation (academic, health, financial, social).
  4. Analyze persistence and "grit" as learned behaviors, not fixed traits, weigh the criticisms of the idea, and plan for likely setbacks.
  5. Create a Personal Student Success Plan that integrates all four weeks.

items.title: Desired outcomes
items.text:
• A well-being check-in naming your sleep and stress baseline and two concrete recovery strategies you'll use.
  • A resources map listing at least 3 relevant supports (academic advising or tutoring, health or counseling, financial, peer or community).
  • A setback plan: "If I get a bad grade / a crisis / a low week, my first three moves are…"
  • A persistence note: one past setback reframed, plus a one-sentence self-compassion script you can use next time.
  • The capstone: a one- to two-page Personal Student Success Plan integrating mindset, study strategy, weekly system, and well-being, with a 30/60/90-day view (template at the end of this document).

items.title: Sessions
items.text:
• Session 1 — The Body in the Room (≈65 min)
  • Session 2 — Regulation That Works (≈60 min)
  • Session 3 — You Don't Have to Do It Alone (≈60 min)
  • Session 4 — Persistence & the Capstone (≈90 min)

items.title: Capstone template: Personal Student Success Plan (1–2 pages)
items.text:
1. My motivation (2–3 sentences). Why I'm here, in my own words. Sample start: "I'm doing this because…"
  2. How I learn (Module 1). My top 2 strengths, 2 challenges, and the workaround I trust most. One growth reframe I'll use when I get stuck.
  3. How I study (Module 2). My top 3 strategies, each with a use-case. Sample: "Retrieval practice: after each reading, close the book and write what I remember."
  4. How I run my week (Module 3). My planner and note system, my weekly plan skeleton (fixed commitments, focus blocks, buffer), my Sunday reset time, and my first move when I catch myself procrastinating (my if–then plan).
  5. How I stay well (Module 4). My sleep target, my two recovery strategies, my early warning signs, and my top 3 supports with how to use each.
  6. If things go wrong. My first three moves after a bad grade, a crisis, or a low week.
  7. 30 / 60 / 90 days. | | Focus | Instructions | |---|---|---| | Day 30 | Make the routines stick | "Do the Sunday reset 4 weeks in a row. Complete one full Day 1 / 3 / 7 spaced cycle for [subject]. Keep the sleep log going." | | Day 60 | Test and adjust | "Run one exam or assignment prep plan end to end and write the post-mortem. Cut one low-value habit. Check in with my accountability partner." | | Day 90 | Audit and rewrite | "Repeat the time audit. Compare with Week 3. Rewrite this plan, keeping what worked." |
  8. Accountability. Who will I share this with, and when will I check in?

items.title: Overview
items.text: Overview

items.title: Module 1 — Foundations & Mindset: "Who Am I as a Learner?"
items.text: STU-101 · Student Success 101 · self-directed lesson plan

items.title: Week at a glance
items.text:
Theme Before technique, identity. You can't regulate learning you haven't examined. Time About 4½ hours of core work: a 10-minute start-of-week check, four sessions of 55–65 minutes, and a 20-minute end-of-week self-check. Optional readings, videos, and partner steps add roughly 2 more hours; pick what helps, you don't need them all. Times in parentheses include the optional items. CLOs 1 (Model self), 2 (Growth mindset), 3 (Goals & self-regulation) Capstone deposits "About Me as a Learner" profile · reframe card · motivation statement · SMART goals sheet with Zimmerman placement · Zimmerman cycle sheet Works with Alone, with a study buddy, or live with a group

How every session works. Each session follows the same six steps so you always know what comes next:

  1. A 5-minute warm-up from memory (from Session 2 on)
  2. The core ideas
  3. A reading or video with a link and time estimate
  4. The activity, with a solo version and an optional partner version
  5. A deposit toward your capstone project
  6. Options for how to do it (written, audio, or letter) A no-tech version is always available: paper, a pen, and a timer. Every handout ends with a worked example so you can see what "specific enough" looks like.

Who this is for. This course works whether you are in school, in job training, or learning on your own. When a prompt says "course," read it as any class, training, certification, or project where you were learning something. You don't need to be enrolled anywhere to take it.

items.title: Desired outcomes
items.text:
• A written "About Me as a Learner" profile naming at least 2 strengths, 2 challenges, 1 helpful or harmful condition, and 1 current workaround, plus your "why" in one sentence and one thing you're curious about.
  • One reframe card where a fixed "I can't" statement becomes "I can't yet, and here's the path."
  • A rating of your autonomy, competence, and relatedness, one small step to strengthen your weakest need, and a one-paragraph motivation statement ("why I'm here").
  • A SMART goals sheet with at least 3 goals, each with a metric, a deadline, and a first action step (one goal developed in full).
  • A Zimmerman placement for each goal (forethought, performance, or self-reflection) and a description of the next loop for your main goal.
  • A one-page Zimmerman cycle sheet for one real goal: forethought (goal and plan), performance (strategy and how you'll monitor), and self-reflection (what worked, what to change).

items.title: Learning objectives
items.text:
By the end of this week, you will be able to:

  1. Identify your own learning profile: strengths, challenges, the conditions that help or hurt, and workarounds you already use.
  2. Describe at least two ways your beliefs about ability (fixed vs. growth) shape your choices and persistence.
  3. Apply growth-mindset reframing to a real setback.
  4. Create at least three SMART goals for the next 4–12 weeks (one developed in full), and tell a process goal from an outcome goal.
  5. Explain the three phases of Zimmerman's self-regulation cycle and place each of your goals within it.

items.title: Start of week (10 min)
items.text: Rate your confidence from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very) on each of the five learning objectives above, and write the numbers down. You'll re-rate at the end of the week; the change is your evidence of progress.

items.title: Time budget
items.text: Session Warm-up Learn Do Total 1 · The Learner Inventory — 20 (45) min 40 (45) min ≈60 (90) min 2 · Mindset: Fixed vs. Growth 5 min 15 (35) min 35 (40) min ≈55 (80) min 3 · Motivation That Lasts 5 min 15 (45) min 35 min ≈55 (85) min 4 · Goals & Self-Regulation 5 min 15 (45) min 45 (50) min ≈65 (100) min End of week self check = 20 min

items.title: End-of-week self-check (20 min)
items.text:
Answer from memory first (15 min), then check your notes and the answers below.

  1. Name the three phases of Zimmerman's cycle and one thing you would do in each.
  2. What are the three needs in Self-Determination Theory?
  3. Rewrite "I'm just bad at this" using the three-move reframe.
  4. What makes a goal SMART, and what is the difference between a process goal and an outcome goal?
  5. What is a "false growth mindset"?

Answers

  1. Forethought: plan and anticipate obstacles; Performance: do it and monitor; Self-reflection: compare to the goal and adjust.
  2. Autonomy, competence, relatedness.
  3. Add "yet," name a next step, connect to a resource.
  4. Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound; a process goal is the behavior you'll do, an outcome goal is the result you want.
  5. Using growth-mindset language without changing what you do. Then refine your Handout 1-A profile (5 min): add or change at least one entry based on what you learned this week. Finally, re-rate your confidence on the five learning objectives and compare with the start of the week.

items.title: Completion checklist
items.text:
• Handout 1-A: profile complete (including your "why" and what you're curious about) and refined at the end of the week
  • Handout 1-B: at least one reframe card complete
  • Handout 1-C: three needs rated, one small step written for the weakest need, motivation statement written and revised once
  • Handout 1-D: 3+ goals, each with metric, deadline, and first action (Goal 1 complete), plus Zimmerman placement for each
  • Handout 1-E: Zimmerman cycle sheet complete for Goal 1 (placeholder strategy is fine)
  • End-of-week self-check done; confidence re-rated These five handouts are your capstone deposits for Week 4's Personal Student Success Plan.

items.title: Next steps & bridge to Week 2
items.text:
• Bridge to Week 2: bring your learning profile with you. Week 2's study strategies (retrieval, spacing, SQ3R, active notes) will be chosen from your actual challenges, not assigned blindly. If you flagged "I cram and re-read," spacing comes first. If you flagged "I can't make sense of dense text," the reading routine comes first.
  • Return to Handout 1-E in Week 2: once you've met a strategy you like, swap it in for your placeholder in the Performance box.
  • Habit to keep: the 5-minute bedtime reflection and the weekly prompt.
  • Continued beyond: revisit your motivation statement before every major deadline. It's your reset button.

items.title: Session 1 — The Learner Inventory (≈60 (90) min)
items.text:
Focus: metacognitive self-assessment; identifying your learning profile.

Deposit: "About Me as a Learner" profile (draft).

items.title: Learn (20 (45) min)
items.text:
• Read (20 min): OpenStax College Success, Chapter 2 ("Knowing Yourself as a Learner"). Start with the chapter introduction, then read section 2.1, "The Power to Learn" (metacognition: thinking about your own thinking).
  • Optional read (25 min): Section 2.4, "Learning Styles," in the same chapter. It covers what research says about learning styles and how to use your preferences without being boxed in by them.

items.title: Do (40 (45) min)
items.text:
Four-box inventory (25 min). Think about the last two courses, training programs, or projects you completed (school or work or independently). What made one easier? What made the other harder? Where did you go when you got stuck? Then fill in four boxes:

  1. Strengths
  2. Challenges
  3. Conditions that help or hurt
  4. Workarounds I already use Aim for specific entries, with at least two in Strengths and Challenges and at least one in each of the other two boxes.

Draft your profile (15 min). Move your best entries onto Handout 1-A (found in Module 1's Materials). Then complete the last two rows: your "why" in one sentence (rough is fine; you'll expand it in Session 3) and one thing you're curious about in how you learn.

Optional partner step (5 min): only if you want to, trade handouts with a buddy and each name one strength you didn't expect and one workaround you'd never have labeled as such. You choose what to share; skip anything you'd rather keep private.

items.title: Session 2 — Mindset: Fixed vs. Growth (≈55 (80) min)
items.text:
Focus: Dweck's mindset research; reframing fixed-ability beliefs.

Deposit: reframe card (one real setback, rewritten).

items.title: Warm-up from memory (5 min)
items.text: Without looking: name one strength, one challenge, and one workaround from your Handout 1-A. Then check.

items.title: Learn (15 (35) min)
items.text:
• Watch (10 min): Carol Dweck, "The power of believing that you can improve" (TED).
  • Read (5 min): Carol Dweck, "Carol Dweck Revisits the 'Growth Mindset'" (Education Week, 2015), her own caution about false growth mindset.
  • Optional read (5 min): KQED MindShift, "Carol Dweck Explains The 'False' Growth Mindset That Worries Her."
  • Optional read (15 min): Section 2.3, "It's All in the Mindset," of OpenStax College Success Chapter 2.

items.title: Do (35 (40) min)
items.text:
Language audit (10 min). List your own fixed phrases from the last month ("I'm bad at…", "I'm just not a ___ person," "Some people are just better at this"). Next to each one, jot what it made you avoid, skip, or put off. This is how a belief about ability turns into a choice.

Reframe relay, solo version (25 min). Pick two statements from the starter list below, or your own, and complete a Handout 1-B card for each. Then pick your best reframe and say it aloud once.

Starter statements:

  1. "I'm just not a writer."
  2. "I'll never be good at statistics."
  3. "I'm bad at public speaking, so I'll just avoid group presentations."
  4. "I failed that test, so I clearly don't belong in this field." (Swap in your own: a midterm, a certification practice exam, a work review.)
  5. "I'm just not a numbers person, so I hand off anything with a spreadsheet."
  6. Your own (optional). Partner version (5 min, optional): trade cards with a buddy. Each person reads the other's reframe aloud and asks one follow-up question ("What's the first thing you'll try?"). Share only the statements you're comfortable sharing; you never have to show a card.

items.title: Session 3 — Motivation That Lasts (≈55 (85) min)
items.text:
Focus: intrinsic vs. extrinsic motivation; Self-Determination Theory (SDT); your motivation statement.

Deposit: SDT ratings and motivation statement (one paragraph).

items.title: Warm-up from memory (5 min)
items.text: Write the three-move reframe from memory and apply it to "I can't focus." Then check Handout 1-B.

items.title: Learn (15 (45) min)
items.text:
• Read (15 min): the Center for Self-Determination Theory's "Theory" overview. Read the overview and the part on basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness). It's written in plain language by the theory's home site.
  • Optional skim (15 min): Ryan & Deci (2000), "Self-Determination Theory and the Facilitation of Intrinsic Motivation, Social Development, and Well-Being." The original research article. Read the introduction and the section on psychological needs and mental health, then skip the rest if you wish.
  • Optional watch (15 min): Scott Geller, "The psychology of self-motivation" (TEDxVirginiaTech).

items.title: Do (35 min)
items.text:
Rate your three needs (5 min). On Handout 1-C, rate your autonomy, competence, and relatedness in your current studies or work (1 = very low, 5 = very high), add one reason for each rating, circle your weakest need, and write one small thing that would strengthen it this week.

Answer the scaffolding prompts (5 min). Jot short answers to the five prompts on Handout 1-C.

Write your motivation statement (15 min). One paragraph, 4–8 sentences, answering: Why am I here, and what do I want the next stretch to feel like? You can mention family, community, faith, career, curiosity, a past failure you want to reverse, or a future version of yourself. Aim for honesty rather than impression: if a sentence sounds like something you'd say in a job interview, ask whether it's really true for you, and say it the way you'd say it to a friend. If you're stuck, use the three SDT questions on the handout:

  • (a) What do I want to choose?
  • (b) What skill do I want to improve?
  • © Who do I want to be around while I do this? Use your weakest need to guide you.

Read it back (5 min). Read it aloud to yourself (or a buddy, if you like). Does it sound like you, or like a cover letter? Revise once.

Self-check (5 min).

  • Is it in my voice?
  • Does it mention at least one specific thing (a course, a skill, a person, a goal)?
  • Can I read it back and recognize myself in it?

items.title: Session 4 — Goals & Self-Regulation (≈65 (100) min)
items.text:
Focus: SMART goals; process vs. outcome goals; Zimmerman's self-regulation cycle; the weekly reflection prompt. CLOs: 3 (primary), 1 (applied).

Deposit: SMART goals sheet (3+ goals) with Zimmerman placement, and a Zimmerman cycle sheet for one goal.

items.title: Warm-up from memory (5 min)
items.text: Name the three needs in Self-Determination Theory and say which one is weakest for you right now (check your Handout 1-C rating). Then check your notes.

items.title: Learn (15 (45) min)
items.text:
• Read (10 min): Purdue Global Academic Success Center, "Teaching Students to Learn." A short, free overview of the three phases of self-regulation, with quotes from Zimmerman. It is written for faculty, so read it for the phases and examples.
  • Core idea (5 min): SMART goals, and process vs. outcome. A SMART goal is:
  • Specific (what exactly?)
  • Measurable (how will you know?)
  • Achievable (challenging but doable given your load)
  • Relevant (tied to your "why")
  • Time-bound (it has a deadline) Goals also come in two kinds. An outcome goal is the result you want ("pass the certification exam"). A process goal is the behavior you control ("study three evenings a week"). Outcomes depend partly on things you can't control, so pair each outcome goal with a process goal. Handout 1-D has a row for checking which kind you wrote.
  • Optional read (30 min): Zimmerman (2002), "Becoming a Self-Regulated Learner: An Overview" (Theory Into Practice).

items.title: Do (45 (50) min)
items.text:
1. Build your SMART goals sheet (20 min). Choose three goals for the next 4–12 weeks. They don't all have to be academic: one can be well-being, one social, one a skill. Fill in every row for the goal you most want to keep (Goal 1). For Goals 2 and 3, fill in at least the metric, the deadline, and a first action step you can do within 48 hours; you can come back for the other rows later. Use Handout 1-D.
  2. Place each goal in the cycle (5 min). For each goal, mark forethought, performance, or self-reflection. For Goal 1, write what the next loop looks like. (Most goals set this week are in forethought. That's fine.)
  3. Complete a Zimmerman cycle sheet for Goal 1 (10 min). Fill in Handout 1-E. In the strategy box, a placeholder is fine (for example, "a timed 25-minute block"). Week 2 gives you real study strategies, and you'll swap one in then.
  4. Check your obstacle for a hidden belief (5 min). Look at the obstacle you named on Handout 1-E. If it hides a fixed statement ("I'm just not a morning person," "I always lose motivation"), run it through a Handout 1-B card: add "yet," name a next step, connect a resource. If it's purely practical (no quiet space, not enough time), skip the card and use the five minutes to sharpen your if–then.
  5. Set up your rhythms (5 min). Put the weekly reflection prompt where you'll see it, and set a reminder for the 5-minute bedtime reflection starting tonight. Partner version (5 min, optional): trade sheets and ask one question per goal: "How will you measure that?" or "What might get in the way?" Share only what you're comfortable sharing.
